In [[geometry]], '''Hessenberg varieties''', first studied by Filippo De Mari, [[Claudio Procesi]], and Mark A. Shayman, are [[Algebraic variety|subvarieties]] of the full [[flag variety]] that are defined in terms of a Hessenberg function ''h'' and a linear transformation&nbsp;''X''.  The study of Hessenberg varieties was first motivated by questions in [[numerical analysis]] in relation to algorithms for computing eigenvalues and eigenspaces of the linear operator&nbsp;''X''.  Later work by [[T. A. Springer]], Dale Peterson, [[Bertram Kostant]], among others, found connections with [[combinatorics]], [[representation theory]] and [[cohomology]].

== Definitions ==
A ''Hessenberg function'' is a map 

:<math>h :\{1,2, \ldots,n \} \rightarrow \{1,2, \ldots,n \}</math> 

such that 

:<math> h(i+1) \geq \text{max }(i,h(i))</math>

for each ''i''. For example, the function that sends the numbers 1 to 5 (in order) to 2, 3, 3, 4, and 5 is a Hessenberg function.

For any Hessenberg function ''h'' and a linear transformation 

:<math> X: \Complex^n \rightarrow \Complex^n, \, </math>

the ''Hessenberg variety'' <math>\mathcal{H}(X,h)</math> is the set of all [[Flag (linear algebra)|flag]]s <math> F_{\bullet} </math> such that 

:<math> X \cdot F_i \subseteq F_{h(i)} </math> 

for all ''i''.

== Examples ==
Examples of Hessenberg varieties (with their <math>h</math> functions) include:

The full flag variety: ''h''(''i'') = ''n'' for all ''i''.

The [[Peterson variety]]: <math>h(i) = i+1</math> for <math> i = 1,2,\dots, n-1.</math>

The [[Springer variety]]: <math> h(i) = i </math> for all <math> i.</math>
